Chapter Two: Understanding Old Patterns—How Family Shapes Our Relationships.
Have you ever noticed how every family has its own unique way of dealing with closeness, distance, and even conflict? Some families are open books—they talk about everything. Others? They keep certain things locked up tight. Maybe you grew up in a family that celebrated independence, or perhaps loyalty and togetherness were the highest priorities.
The thing is, these patterns don’t just disappear when we leave home. They follow us, quietly shaping the way we handle love, anger, and vulnerability as adults.
Picture this: there’s a woman who’s always felt like she’s responsible for her mother’s happiness. Even now, as an adult, she finds herself dropping everything to answer her mom’s calls, rearranging her own life just to avoid causing disappointment. She tells herself, “That’s just what daughters do.” But deep down, she wonders—why do my own needs always come last?
That sense of obligation didn’t just appear out of nowhere. It was built over years of little moments—being praised for helping out, getting a look of disappointment when she stood up for herself, or feeling relief whenever she smoothed things over. Little by little, she learned her role was to be the “good daughter”—the one who never made waves. Now, setting boundaries feels almost impossible, because she’s scared that any sign of independence will look like betrayal.
Family patterns are powerful, mostly because they’re so familiar. Most of us don’t question them—we just repeat what we know. If someone grew up with a distant father, for example, they might find themselves drawn to partners who are emotionally unavailable, hoping to finally win the love they missed. And if you were raised in a family where anger was never allowed? You might struggle to express frustration, turning it inward instead.
These patterns aren’t just about our personal choices—they’re woven into the fabric of family life. When someone tries to break the mold, the whole system pushes back. The daughter who starts saying “no” might be met with guilt or even anger. Or a partner who asks for more space could be accused of being selfish. The pressure to slip back into old roles? It can be intense.
But here’s the encouraging part: change is possible, even in families where patterns feel totally set. It starts with simply noticing the scripts we’ve inherited—who gets to speak, who stays quiet, and who’s expected to take care of everyone else. It means asking tough questions, like: Whose needs always come first? What happens if someone disagrees? How is love shown, and what’s left unsaid?
Let me give you an example. One woman, after years of feeling trapped by her family’s expectations, decided to do things differently. Instead of automatically saying yes to every request, she started pausing—checking in with herself. Sometimes she agreed, but other times, she gently declined. At first, her family pushed back, calling her cold or ungrateful. But as she stood her ground, something started to shift. She felt more present, less resentful. Her relationships didn’t fall apart—they actually became more honest.
Most of us underestimate just how much our family history shapes the present. The urge to repeat old patterns is strong—but so is the desire for something better. When we bring these patterns into the light, we give ourselves the chance to choose a different path. Not by rejecting the past, but by understanding it—and deciding what we want to carry forward.
